title: DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT STILL GIVE SPIRITUAL GIFTS TODAY?
paragraphs:
DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT STILL GIVE SPIRITUAL GIFTS TODAY?
Tongues. Prophecy. Healing. Miracles. Discernment. Have They Ceased—or Have We Become So Afraid of Counterfeits That We No Longer Expect the Spirit to Move?
There is a strange tension in the modern church.
Some Christians seem willing to believe almost anything as long as someone says, “The Holy Spirit told me.”
Others become uncomfortable the moment someone mentions prophecy, healing, tongues, miracles, or supernatural gifts.
One side can become so hungry for manifestations that discernment disappears.
The other can become so frightened of deception that expectation disappears.
And somewhere between the sensationalism and the skepticism stands an uncomfortable question:
Does the Holy Spirit still give spiritual gifts today?
Not...
“Have I seen something convincing?”
Not...
“What does my denomination teach?”
Not even...
“What happened at that conference?”
The deeper question is:
What does Scripture actually give us permission to believe?
Because your experience is not the final authority.
Neither is mine.
A preacher is not.
A church tradition is not.
A viral testimony is not.
A spectacular miracle video is not.
And neither is a disappointing experience in which you prayed desperately and nothing seemed to happen.
The Word of God must judge our experiences rather than our experiences rewriting the Word of God.
And when Paul writes to the Corinthians about spiritual gifts, he uses a word that should immediately humble all of us:
χαρίσματα — charismata.
It comes from the same family of words associated with χάρις — charis — grace.
Gifts of grace.
That matters.
Because spiritual gifts were never supposed to become spiritual trophies.
They were never given so Christians could build celebrity identities around themselves.
They were never intended to create a hierarchy in which one believer says, “God uses me more than He uses you.”
They are gifts.
Grace given.
Grace distributed.
Grace that leaves no room for boasting.
Paul writes:
Then comes the sentence that destroys spiritual pride:
“But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.”
—1 Corinthians 12:8–11
The Greek behind that final thought is striking:
καθὼς βούλεται — kathōs bouletai
“As He wills.”
Not as the preacher wills.
Not as the congregation demands.
Not as the person seeking a platform decides.
As the Spirit wills.
And perhaps that is where this conversation needs to begin.
The Holy Spirit is not a force Christians learn to control.
He is God.
He is sovereign.

Jesus spoke of the Holy Spirit personally, not as an impersonal spiritual electricity. The Spirit teaches, testifies, guides, glorifies Christ, convicts, distributes gifts, intercedes, and can be grieved.
And if our fascination with spiritual gifts becomes greater than our fascination with Jesus Christ, something has already gone terribly wrong.
Jesus said of the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me.”
—John 16:14
That may be one of the most important tests in this entire discussion.
Does what we are calling a movement of the Holy Spirit magnify Jesus—or magnify the person claiming to possess the gift?
Because the Spirit who inspired Scripture will never contradict the Scripture He inspired.
The Spirit who glorifies Christ will never lead us away from Christ.
The Spirit of truth will never require us to abandon truth in order to experience Him.
And yet...
We must be equally careful about making the opposite mistake.
The existence of counterfeit money does not prove real money does not exist.
False prophecy does not logically prove that God can never graciously work through spiritual gifts.
Fraudulent healers do not prove God cannot heal.
Emotional manipulation does not prove every powerful spiritual experience is manipulation.
Paul knew churches could mishandle spiritual gifts.
The Corinthian church certainly did.
And his solution is fascinating.
He does not simply tell them:
“Stop everything supernatural.”
Instead, he corrects them.
Orders them.
Centers them on love.
Demands intelligibility.
Requires discernment.
And repeatedly redirects attention away from personal exhibition and toward the building up of Christ’s church.
Paul says:
“Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant.”
—1 Corinthians 12:1
Then later:
“Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.”
—1 Corinthians 14:1
The Greek is even more forceful:
ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά — zēloute de ta pneumatika
Earnestly desire spiritual things or spiritual gifts.
And near the end of the chapter Paul says:
“Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order.”
—1 Corinthians 14:39–40
Notice the balance.
Do not forbid.
But also:
Decently and in order.
That is uncomfortable for extremists on both sides.
The Christian who accepts every supernatural claim without examination must deal with Scripture's commands concerning discernment.
The Christian who dismisses every claim automatically must deal with Scripture's warning not to despise prophecy.
Paul tells the Thessalonians:
“Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:19–21
That is astonishingly balanced Christianity.
Do not quench.
Do not despise.
But test.
The Greek verb translated “prove” or “test” is:
δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete
Test.
Examine.
Discern what is genuine.
Biblical faith is not gullibility.
You do not have to switch off your discernment to believe in the supernatural.
In fact, Scripture commands the opposite.
John writes:
—1 John 4:1
That single verse destroys the idea that questioning a claimed supernatural revelation is somehow resisting God.
God Himself commands examination.
If someone tells you, “Don't question me; I am anointed,” you have already been given biblical reason to become cautious.
If someone claims God told them something that contradicts Scripture, Scripture wins.
Every time.

If someone uses supposed spiritual authority to manipulate people, enrich themselves, excuse sexual immorality, control relationships, predict things falsely, or make themselves functionally unquestionable, their charisma should never override biblical truth.
The Holy Spirit does not need deception to accomplish the work of God.
But this brings us to the difficult part.
Some sincere, Bible-believing Christians argue that certain miraculous gifts were uniquely associated with the apostolic era and ceased after their foundational purpose had been fulfilled.
This position is commonly called cessationism.

Other sincere, Bible-believing Christians argue that Scripture never explicitly teaches that all such gifts cease before Christ's return and therefore believe God may continue distributing them according to His sovereign will.
This is commonly called continuationism.
Christians on both sides have attempted to ground their conclusions in Scripture.
And we should represent each other honestly.

Cessationists frequently point to the unique foundational role of the apostles, the signs associated with apostolic ministry, the foundational language of Ephesians 2:20, and passages such as Hebrews 2:3–4. Some also understand 1 Corinthians 13 as compatible with the eventual cessation of revelatory or sign gifts.

Continuationists respond that no New Testament passage unambiguously says all miraculous gifts will disappear with the death of the apostles or the completion of the biblical canon. They point especially to Paul's instructions concerning gifts, Peter's Pentecost sermon, and the language of 1 Corinthians 13.
That passage deserves careful attention.
Paul writes:
Someone might stop there and say:
“There it is. They cease.”
Yes.
Paul absolutely says they cease.
The question is when.
He continues:
“For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.”
—1 Corinthians 13:8–10
Then Paul describes the present condition:
“For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.”
—1 Corinthians 13:12
The Greek phrase translated “face to face” is:
πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον — prosōpon pros prosōpon
Face to face.
Continuationists commonly understand Paul's language as pointing toward the consummation when believers encounter Christ in fullness rather than toward the closing of the biblical canon.
Cessationists offer different readings and emphasize the temporary and partial nature of these gifts together with the unique foundational period of the apostles.
We should therefore resist pretending the debate can be settled by shouting one isolated verse louder than everyone else.
But there is something both sides desperately need to hear.
You can win an argument about spiritual gifts...
and still grieve the Holy Spirit.
You can have flawless cessationist theology and be proud, loveless, prayerless, cold, bitter, and spiritually asleep.
You can have passionate continuationist theology and be undiscerning, manipulative, disorderly, obsessed with experiences, and hungry for manifestations instead of holiness.
And Paul places something right in the middle of his teaching on gifts that should terrify both camps.
First Corinthians 12 discusses gifts.
First Corinthians 14 discusses gifts.
And sitting between them is First Corinthians 13.
Love.
That is not an accident we should rush past.
Paul says you could speak with extraordinary tongues...
and without love become noise.
You could prophesy.
Understand mysteries.
Possess remarkable knowledge.
Exercise astonishing faith.
And still be...
nothing.
Think about that.
A person could appear spiritually spectacular and still be spiritually hollow.
Because the greatest evidence of God's work in your life is not how impressive you appear in a church service.
Paul also speaks of something far less glamorous:
“The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance.”
—Galatians 5:22–23
Maybe someone needs to hear this.
You have been asking God for a gift people can see...
while He has been trying to produce fruit nobody applauds.
Patience when you are provoked.
Purity when nobody is watching.
Forgiveness toward the person who wounded you.
Self-control when temptation whispers.
Kindness toward someone who cannot repay you.
Faithfulness when serving feels invisible.
Love when bitterness would be easier.
Those things will probably never make you famous.
But heaven notices.
And there is an even deeper danger.
We can become so fascinated with the gifts of the Spirit that we neglect the greatest gift God has given us:
Jesus Christ Himself.
Before you argue about whether someone can speak in tongues...
Have you spoken honestly to Jesus about your sin?
Before you chase prophecy...
Are you obeying what God has already revealed in Scripture?
Before you search for signs...
Have you looked at the cross?
Before you ask whether God still heals bodies...
Have you allowed the Gospel to expose the disease of sin in your own heart?
Because Christianity is not ultimately about obtaining supernatural abilities.
Christianity is about reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
We were not separated from God because we lacked spiritual gifts.
We were separated because of sin.
And Christ did not come primarily to turn ordinary people into impressive religious performers.
He came to save sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is not that broken people can become powerful.
The scandal is that a holy God would show mercy to rebels.
That the innocent Son of God would stand where the guilty belonged.
That Christ would bear sin.
That the King would wear thorns.
That the hands through which creation came would be pierced by His creation.
That Jesus would die...
and rise again.
This is where every spiritual gift must eventually kneel.
At the cross.
Because you can pursue supernatural experiences and still miss the Savior.
Jesus Himself gave one of Scripture's most sobering warnings:
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?... and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
Yet He warns that miraculous claims are not, by themselves, proof that someone belongs to Him.
—Matthew 7:22–23
That should shake us.
The question is not merely:
“What gifts do you have?”
The deeper question is:
“Does Jesus have you?”
Maybe you have spent years arguing about the Holy Spirit while quietly resisting Him.
Maybe nobody knows about the pornography.
The bitterness.
The secret relationship.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The resentment.
The religious performance.
The hidden compromise.
You can debate Greek words and still hide from God.
You can know every theological argument and still need repentance.
And perhaps the most supernatural thing that could happen in your life tonight is not falling to the floor.
Maybe it is finally falling to your knees.
Maybe it is whispering:
“Jesus... I have been pretending.”
Maybe the miracle you desperately need begins with repentance.
Because the Holy Spirit does not merely distribute gifts.
He glorifies Christ.
He convicts concerning sin.
He produces fruit.
He empowers witness.
He sanctifies God's people.
He leads believers toward truth.
And genuine spiritual life will ultimately make Jesus larger in your vision and self smaller.
So, does the Holy Spirit still give spiritual gifts today?

Christians who affirm the continuing operation of the gifts have substantial biblical reasons for believing the Spirit remains free to distribute gifts according to His will, and Scripture contains no universally agreed-upon verse explicitly stating that every miraculous gift must cease with the death of the apostles.

Christians who believe some gifts ceased rightly remind the church that the apostles occupied a unique foundational role and that extraordinary claims must never be allowed to compete with the final authority of Scripture.
Wherever you land, several truths should remain immovable:
Christ is Lord.
Scripture is authoritative.
The Gospel cannot be altered.
The Holy Spirit glorifies Jesus.
Spiritual claims must be tested.
Gifts must never become grounds for pride.
Everything in gathered worship should seek the edification of Christ's body.
Love is indispensable.
Holiness matters.
And salvation comes through Jesus Christ—not through possessing any particular spiritual gift.
You are not saved because you speak in tongues.
You are not saved because you do not speak in tongues.
You are not saved because you have experienced healing.
You are not saved because your theology of healing is perfectly formulated.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And if God gives gifts, they belong to Him.
If He heals, the glory belongs to Him.
If He gives wisdom, the glory belongs to Him.
If He empowers someone to serve, teach, encourage, give, lead, show mercy, discern, or minister in extraordinary ways...
the glory belongs to Him.
Always.
Perhaps the better prayer is therefore not:
“Holy Spirit, make me impressive.”
But:
“Holy Spirit, make me useful to Jesus.”
Use my mouth.
Use my hands.
Use my weakness.
Use my testimony.
Use the parts of my story I wish had never happened.
Use the scars.
Use the failures You redeemed.
Use everything.
Just let Jesus be seen.
Because this is what grace does.
Grace walks into stories we thought were ruined and writes redemption across pages covered in shame.
Peter denied Christ...
and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians...
and became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The Corinthians were confused, divided, immature, and disorderly...
yet Paul still called them toward holiness, love, truth, and the proper use of what God had given.
Maybe your story feels equally disqualified.
It isn't beyond Christ's reach.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority over the Author.
Jesus does.
So whether you have spent your life in a charismatic church, a cessationist church, no church at all, or somewhere painfully between belief and doubt...
come back to Jesus.
Not hype.
Not personalities.
Not denominations.
Not experiences.
Not cynicism.
Jesus.

And if God has brought you through confusion, church hurt, spiritual deception, or seasons of doubt, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need to discover that struggling with questions does not mean they have to run away from Christ.
Send it privately to the believer who is afraid to ask.

But if these resources genuinely strengthen your walk with Jesus and you want to help us reach more people with biblical content, your support can become an act of generosity and stewardship offered for God's glory.
Do not leave Jesus outside the locked rooms of your life.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Test what claims to be spiritual.
Return to Scripture.
Pursue love.
Seek holiness.
Ask God to make your life useful.
And whatever gifts He chooses to give—or does not choose to give—never confuse the gift with the Giver.
Because one day tongues will be silent.
Prophecies will no longer be needed.
Faith will become sight.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
So do not spend your whole life chasing the supernatural only to overlook the Savior standing at the center of it all.
“Jesus, lead me into truth.”
Sometimes the greatest evidence that the Holy Spirit is moving is not that a person becomes louder—but that a sinner stops running, turns toward the cross, and finally comes home.
